title: Jñāneśvarī (Bhāvārthadīpikā)
summary: Jñāneśvar's Old Marathi verse (ovī) commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā, expanding each verse with images from village life. It teaches non-dual knowledge crowned by devotion, gives a celebrated account of kuṇḍalinī yoga in chapter 6 (the 'royal road', pantharāja), names its Nāth lineage from Ādinātha to Nivṛttināth, and closes with the prayer for grace (Pasāydān). It is the first of the three foundational books of the Vārkarīs.

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Jñāneśvar at Nevāse before an assembly, with Nivṛttināth present, and written down by Saccidānanda Bābā (colophon, ch. 18).
attribution.scholarly: Accepted as Jñāneśvar's; the transmitted text passed through Eknāth's corrected recension (1584). A minority of scholars distinguish the author of the Jñāneśvarī from the author of the abhaṅgas ascribed to 'Jñānadev'.

tradition.text: Śaka 1212 (1290 CE), stated in the colophon

structure.description: 18 chapters following the Gītā; about 9,000 ovīs (c. 9,030–9,040 depending on edition)

editions.name: Eknāth's recension (Śaka 1506 / 1584 CE), basis of the vulgate

title: Amṛtānubhava (Anubhavāmṛta)
summary: Jñāneśvar's independent work on non-dual experience: after saluting Śiva and Śakti as one and praising his guru Nivṛtti, it argues that the words sat, cit and ānanda, the word itself, ignorance and even knowledge fail before the self-luminous reality, which sports as the world; it ends in a devotion in which God, devotee and worship are one.

attribution.tradition: Written at Nivṛttināth's bidding as an independent work (svatantra grantha) after the commentary.

tradition.text: shortly after the Jñāneśvarī

title: Cāṅgadeva Pāsaṣṭī
summary: Jñāneśvar's letter of sixty-five ovīs to the aged yogī Cāṅgadev: the self is one, like gold in all ornaments; knower, knowing and known are one reality; addressing it as 'you' or 'I' already divides it.

attribution.tradition: Cāṅgadev, unable to decide how to address the boy-sage, sent a blank letter; Muktābāī remarked that after fourteen hundred years he was still blank, and Jñāneśvar answered in 65 ovīs.

title: Haripāṭh (of Jñāneśvar)
summary: Twenty-seven (in some editions twenty-eight) abhaṅgas on reciting the name of Hari, recited daily by Vārkarīs: the name needs no rule of time, place or caste; standing a moment at God's door wins the four liberations.

attribution.scholarly: Traditional attribution; not seriously contested but linked to the abhaṅga-authorship question.

notes: Nāmdev, Eknāth and Tukārām are also credited with Haripāṭh cycles; this id is Jñāneśvar's.

title: Jñāneśvar's abhaṅgas (Jñānadev Gāthā)
summary: The devotional lyrics ascribed to Jñāneśvar: praise of Viṭṭhala's form at Paṇḍharpūr, songs of the soul as a longing woman (virahiṇī), and songs of non-dual experience.

attribution.scholarly: Some scholars assign part or all of the abhaṅgas to a later 'Jñānadev'; unresolved.

title: Nāmdev Gāthā
summary: The Marathi abhaṅgas ascribed to Nāmdev (some 2,500) — childhood intimacy with Viṭṭhala, the name and kīrtan, the saints of his circle, the Tīrthāvaḷī (pilgrimage with Jñāneśvar) and the Samādhi songs on Jñāneśvar's entering samādhi — together with his Hindi padas, some of which are preserved in the Sikh scripture (context only).

attribution.tradition: Nāmdev's; he vowed to compose a hundred crore abhaṅgas and his household (Janābāī) completed them.
attribution.scholarly: A large corpus with layers; several later Nāmdevs (e.g. Viṣṇudās Nāmā) may be mixed in.

tradition.text: Nāmdev 1270–1350

title: Tīrthāvaḷī (of Nāmdev)
summary: The section of Nāmdev's abhaṅgas narrating his pilgrimage with Jñāneśvar to the holy places of the north; Nāmdev is reluctant to leave Viṭṭhala, and the saints' company is shown to be the true tīrtha.

title: Janābāī's abhaṅgas
summary: Some three hundred abhaṅgas ascribed to Janābāī, maidservant in Nāmdev's household: Viṭṭhala grinds and pounds grain with her, and songs of work become worship; some songs are non-dual.

attribution.tradition: Janābāī's (many preserved within the Nāmdev Gāthā).

title: Cokhāmeḷā's abhaṅgas
summary: Some three hundred abhaṅgas ascribed to Cokhāmeḷā, a Mahār (then 'untouchable') devotee of Maṅgaḷveḍhe, and to his family (Soyrābāī, Karmameḷā, Nirmaḷā, Bankā): love of Viṭṭhala, the pain of being kept from the temple, and the claim that outward birth does not touch inner devotion.

attribution.scholarly: Traditional attribution; some songs are later.

tradition.text: Cokhāmeḷā died c. 1338

title: Soyrābāī's abhaṅgas
summary: Abhaṅgas ascribed to Soyrābāī, Cokhāmeḷā's wife: the body called impure is the Lord's dwelling, and in devotion all colours become one colour.

structure.description: some sixty to ninety abhaṅgas (count uncertain)

title: Sāvatā Mālī's abhaṅgas
summary: A small group of abhaṅgas by the gardener-saint of Araṇ, who worshipped through his work in the vegetable plot: onion, radish and greens are all Viṭṭhala.

title: Gorā Kumbhār's abhaṅgas
summary: About twenty abhaṅgas by the potter-saint of Terḍhokī, largely on the formless (nirguṇa) within the formed.

title: Eknāthī Bhāgavat
summary: Eknāth's great Marathi ovī commentary on the eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Kṛṣṇa's teaching to Uddhava and the nine sages' teaching to Nimi): devotion to the name, the guru and the saints, the avadhūta's twenty-four teachers, and non-dual knowledge, with a defence of teaching in Marathi. It is the second of the Vārkarīs' three foundational books.

attribution.tradition: Begun at Paiṭhaṇ and completed at Vārāṇasī (Maṇikarṇikā), where it was honoured by the paṇḍits.

tradition.text: completed Śaka 1495 (1573 CE)

structure.description: 31 chapters on Bhāgavata 11; about 18,800 ovīs (count approximate)

title: Bhāvārtha Rāmāyaṇa
summary: Eknāth's long Marathi Rāmāyaṇa in ovīs, telling the story with devotional and inner meanings; left unfinished at his death and completed by his disciple Gāvbā.

attribution.tradition: Eknāth's; the last part (from within the Yuddha-kāṇḍa) by Gāvbā.

title: Rukmiṇī-svayaṃvara (of Eknāth)
summary: Eknāth's ovī poem on Rukmiṇī's marriage to Kṛṣṇa (Bhāgavata 10.52–54), read as the soul's choosing of God; sung at weddings.

title: Eknāth's bhāruḍs
summary: About three hundred bhāruḍs — dramatic allegorical folk songs in the voices of village characters (the scorpion-bitten man, the Jogī, the madwoman, the Mahār) — teaching dispassion, devotion and knowledge to ordinary people.

attribution.scholarly: Accepted for the core; some later imitations.

title: Eknāth Gāthā (abhaṅgas)
summary: Eknāth's abhaṅgas and other lyrics (gauḷaṇ, virahiṇī), including songs on Paṇḍharpūr as his mother's home and on the guru Janārdana.

title: Catuḥślokī Bhāgavata (of Eknāth)
summary: Eknāth's Marathi ovī commentary on the four 'seed' verses of the Bhāgavata (2.9.32–35), in which the Lord teaches Brahmā that he alone was before creation and remains after it.

title: Tukārām Gāthā
summary: The collected abhaṅgas of Tukārām (about 4,500 in the standard editions): confession and struggle, the name 'Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari', Viṭṭhala standing on the brick, scathing attacks on hypocrisy and caste pride, the saints' company, and songs of fulfilment. The third of the Vārkarīs' three foundational books, sung daily in bhajan and kīrtan.

attribution.tradition: Tukārām's; his notebooks, thrown into the Indrāyaṇī at Rāmeśvar Bhaṭṭ's order, rose dry after thirteen days; Santājī Jagnāḍe and others wrote them down.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted core; the corpus was fixed in manuscripts of disciples and printed in 1873 (Bombay government-sponsored edition); some interpolations.

editions.name: Tukārām Gāthā, Indu Prakash / government edition, Bombay 1873

title: Bahiṇābāī's abhaṅgas (with the Ātmanivedana)
summary: The abhaṅgas of Bahiṇābāī of Śiūr, a brahmin woman who took Tukārām as guru in a dream: an autobiography in verse (Ātmanivedana) recounting her marriage, her husband's opposition and her previous births, songs on the true brahmin and the duties of a devoted wife, and the famous image of the saints as a temple.

title: Bhaktavijaya
summary: Mahīpati's ovī hagiography of the saints (Jñāneśvar and his siblings, Nāmdev and his circle, Cokhāmeḷā, Eknāth, Kabīr, Mīrā, Tulsīdās and others), drawing on Nābhājī's Bhaktamāl and Marathi oral tradition; the main source of the saints' miracle-stories as the Vārkarīs tell them.

title: Bhaktalīlāmṛta
summary: Mahīpati's later hagiography, with extended lives of Eknāth and Tukārām.

title: Santalīlāmṛta
summary: Mahīpati's earliest hagiography of the saints.

title: Pāṇḍuraṅga-māhātmya
summary: Glorification of Paṇḍharpūr and of Viṭṭhala: the devotee Puṇḍalīka, absorbed in serving his parents, tosses a brick for the visiting Kṛṣṇa to stand on, and the Lord remains standing on it, hands on hips, ever since.

attribution.tradition: Presented as a section of the Skanda (or Padma) Purāṇa.
attribution.scholarly: Several Sanskrit and Marathi Pāṇḍuraṅga-māhātmyas exist (one Marathi version by the poet Śrīdhara); their Purāṇic placement is not found in the standard printed Purāṇas.

notes: Umbrella id for the Pāṇḍuraṅga-māhātmya texts; individual versions not yet distinguished (see REPORT gaps).

title: Līḷācaritra
summary: The biography of Cakradhar Svāmī in some fifteen hundred short episodes (līḷās), gathered by Mhāimbhaṭ from the disciples' memories after Cakradhar's departure: his acts, conversations, teachings and parables. Revered as scripture by the Mahānubhāvas and counted the earliest prose work in Marathi.

attribution.tradition: Compiled by Mhāimbhaṭ with Nāgadevācārya's approval from the testimony of eyewitnesses.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted; the text survives in several recensions and was long transmitted in the Mahānubhāvas' secret scripts.

structure.description: three parts — Ekāṅka, Pūrvārdha, Uttarārdha — of short episodes (līḷās)

title: Sūtrapāṭh
summary: The sayings of Cakradhar arranged by topic by Keśobās: the four eternal realities (jīva, devatā, prapañca, Parameśvara), the uselessness of worshipping the devatās for liberation, and the conduct of the renunciant (wandering, begging, non-violence, detachment). The Mahānubhāvas' doctrinal scripture.

attribution.tradition: Cakradhar's own words, collected by Keśobās.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted as the earliest digest of Cakradhar's sayings.

structure.description: topical chapters (prakaraṇas) including Vicāra (doctrine) and Ācāra (conduct); exact chapter list and sūtra count to verify

title: Dṛṣṭāntapāṭh
summary: The parables (dṛṣṭānta) Cakradhar used to illustrate his teachings, collected by Keśobās with their applications.

title: Govindaprabhu-caritra (Ṛddhipur-caritra)
summary: Mhāimbhaṭ's collection of episodes of Govindaprabhu (Guṇḍam Rāüḷ) of Ṛddhipur, Cakradhar's guru, whose child-like, unconventional behaviour the Mahānubhāvas read as divine play.

title: Smṛtisthaḷ
summary: Prose memoirs of the Mahānubhāva community after Cakradhar's departure, centred on Nāgadevācārya's leadership and instructions.

attribution.tradition: Collective remembrances of the early disciples.

title: Rukmiṇī-svayaṃvara (of Narendra)
summary: Narendra's ornate Marathi poem on Rukmiṇī's marriage to Kṛṣṇa, one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

title: Śiśupāla-vadha (of Bhāskarabhaṭṭa Borīkar)
summary: Bhāskarabhaṭṭa Borīkar's Marathi poem on Kṛṣṇa's slaying of Śiśupāla, one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

title: Uddhava-gītā / Ekādaśa-skandha (of Bhāskarabhaṭṭa Borīkar)
summary: Bhāskarabhaṭṭa's Marathi rendering of Kṛṣṇa's teaching to Uddhava (Bhāgavata 11), among the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

title: Vatsaharaṇa
summary: Dāmodara Paṇḍita's poem on Brahmā's theft of the calves and cowherd boys (Bhāgavata 10.13), one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

title: Jñānaprabodha
summary: Viśvanātha Bāḷāpurkar's doctrinal poem on Mahānubhāva teaching, one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva works.

title: Sahyādri-varṇana
summary: Ravaḷobās's poem describing the Sahyādri region and the Dattātreya sites (Māhūr), among the seven classic Mahānubhāva works.

title: Ṛddhipura-varṇana
summary: Poem in praise of Ṛddhipur, the town sanctified by Govindaprabhu, counted among the seven classic Mahānubhāva works.

title: Dhavaḷe (of Mahadaisā)
summary: Wedding songs on Rukmiṇī's marriage to Kṛṣṇa by Mahadaisā (Mahadamba), a woman disciple of Cakradhar, counted among the earliest Marathi poems by a woman.

title: Dāsbodh
summary: Samartha Rāmdās's teaching in dialogue between master and disciple: the marks of the fool and the wise, the nine forms of devotion and four kinds of liberation, the true guru and the true disciple, the bound, the seeker, the practitioner and the accomplished, the elements and the discrimination of the self from the non-self, and the conduct of the active leader (mahant) in the world.

attribution.tradition: Dictated by Rāmdās in the cave at Śivthar and written down by Kalyāṇ Svāmī.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted; composed over years in the mid-17th c.

structure.description: 20 daśakas of 10 samāsas each (200 samāsas); about 7,750 ovīs

title: Manāce Śloka
summary: Two hundred and five verses in the bhujaṅgaprayāta metre addressed to one's own mind: go by the path of devotion, hold to Rāma's name, keep good company and inquire who in the world is truly happy.

title: Karuṇāṣṭakeṃ
summary: Rāmdās's plaintive prayers to Rāma, confessing helplessness and asking for grace.

title: Vaiṣṇavamatābjabhāskara
summary: A short Sanskrit treatise attributed to Rāmānanda, answering his disciple Surasurānanda's questions on the supreme reality (Rāma with Sītā), the means (devotion and refuge), the mantra, the marks of the Vaiṣṇava and the goal; it holds refuge in Rāma open to all.

attribution.scholarly: Authenticity disputed; possibly a later Rāmānandī composition.

title: Śrī Rāmārcana-paddhati
summary: A ritual manual for the worship of Rāma attributed to Rāmānanda, with a lineage list (guruparamparā) tracing the Rāmānandīs back through Rāghavānanda.

title: Ānandabhāṣya
summary: A commentary on the Brahma Sūtras (with related commentaries on the Gītā and Upaniṣads) attributed to Rāmānanda by the Rāmānandīs who assert the sect's independence from the Śrīvaiṣṇavas; it reads the Sūtras as teaching a qualified non-dualism centred on Rāma.

attribution.tradition: Rāmānanda's own commentary, recovered and published in the 20th century.
attribution.scholarly: Widely regarded as a 20th-century composition connected with the Rāmānandī independence movement; not attested earlier.

title: Rāmcaritmānas
summary: Tulsīdās's Awadhi retelling of the Rāma story in seven kāṇḍas (Bāla, Ayodhyā, Araṇya, Kiṣkindhā, Sundara, Laṅkā, Uttara), framed by four nested dialogues (Śiva–Pārvatī, Kākabhuśuṇḍi–Garuḍa, Yājñavalkya–Bharadvāja, the poet and his hearers) likened to the four ghāṭs of a lake. It teaches that Rāma is the supreme Brahman, formless and with form; that his name is greater than either form; that devotion (bhakti) with the saints' company is the easiest and surest path in the Kali age; and it depicts dharma embodied in Rāma and Rāma-rājya.

attribution.tradition: Begun by Tulsīdās at Ayodhyā on Rāmanavamī of Saṃvat 1631 (1574 CE) (Bāla-kāṇḍa, near dohā 34) and completed in about two years and seven months; Śiva approved it.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted; draws on the Vālmīki and Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇas, the Bhāgavata, the Hanumannāṭaka and Prasannarāghava.

tradition.text: begun 1574 CE (Saṃvat 1631)

structure.description: 7 kāṇḍas of caupāīs grouped under dohās, with Sanskrit invocatory ślokas at the head of each kāṇḍa; citations here are kāṇḍa.dohā in the Gita Press numbering

title: Vinaya Patrikā
summary: Tulsīdās's 'letter of petition': some 279 devotional songs, opening with hymns to Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Śiva, Devī, Gaṅgā, Hanumān and others before turning to Rāma, confessing the poet's faults and pleading for acceptance.

attribution.tradition: A petition Tulsī presented to Rāma through Hanumān, who had advised it when the Kali age threatened him.

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Kavitāvalī
summary: Tulsīdās's kavitta and savaiyā verses on the Rāma story in seven kāṇḍas; its long Uttara-kāṇḍa contains autobiographical verses, pictures of the Kali age (famine, plague at Vārāṇasī) and professions of dependence on Rāma alone.

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Gītāvalī
summary: Tulsīdās's songs on the Rāma story in seven kāṇḍas, dwelling on tender scenes (the child Rāma, Kausalyā's longing).

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Dohāvalī
summary: A collection of about 570 dohās by Tulsīdās on the name, devotion, conduct and the Kali age, some shared with the Rāmcaritmānas.

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Kṛṣṇa Gītāvalī
summary: Sixty-odd songs by Tulsīdās on Kṛṣṇa's childhood and the gopīs, including a bhramargīt.

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Barvai Rāmāyaṇa
summary: Short barvai-metre verses on the Rāma story in seven kāṇḍas. One of the twelve works generally accepted as Tulsīdās's.

attribution.scholarly: Counted among his twelve accepted works.

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Jānakī Maṅgal
summary: Awadhi maṅgal song on the marriage of Sītā and Rāma. One of the twelve works generally accepted as Tulsīdās's.

attribution.scholarly: Counted among his twelve accepted works.

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Pārvatī Maṅgal
summary: Awadhi maṅgal song on the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī. One of the twelve works generally accepted as Tulsīdās's.

attribution.scholarly: Counted among his twelve accepted works.

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Rāmlalā Nahachū
summary: Folk-style song for the child Rāma's nail-paring ceremony. One of the twelve works generally accepted as Tulsīdās's.

attribution.scholarly: Counted among his twelve accepted works.

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Vairāgya Sandīpanī
summary: Short work in dohās and caupāīs on dispassion and the marks of the saint. One of the twelve works generally accepted as Tulsīdās's.

attribution.scholarly: Counted among his twelve accepted works.

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Rāmājñā Praśna
summary: An omen-book of 343 dohās (7 sargas × 7 saptakas × 7) narrating the Rāma story, used to seek Rāma's command. One of the twelve works generally accepted as Tulsīdās's.

attribution.scholarly: Counted among his twelve accepted works.

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Hanumān Bāhuk
summary: Forty-odd verses addressed to Hanumān, praying for relief from a painful affliction of the arm.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Tulsī in old age when his arm was afflicted; recited against pain.
attribution.scholarly: Generally accepted; sometimes treated as an appendix to the Kavitāvalī.

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Hanumān Cālīsā
summary: Forty caupāīs framed by dohās praising Hanumān as Rāma's servant, messenger and remover of obstacles; opens by cleansing the mirror of the mind with the dust of the guru's feet. The most widely recited Hindi devotional text.

attribution.scholarly: Not among the twelve works accepted in early lists; the attribution is uncertain.

title: Bhaktamāl
summary: Nābhādās's 'garland of devotees': short chappay verses on some two hundred devotees of all ages and sects — from the Purāṇic devotees to the founders of the Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas, Rāmānanda and his twelve disciples, Kabīr, Mīrā, Sūrdās and Tulsīdās — opening with the teaching that devotee, devotion, Lord and guru are one.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Nābhādās at the command of his guru Agradās.

structure.description: about 200 chappays with dohās (numbering differs between editions)

title: Bhaktirasabodhinī
summary: Priyādās's kavitt commentary on the Bhaktamāl, expanding Nābhādās's allusive verses into the full stories of the devotees (Mīrā's poison, Tulsī's encounters, Kabīr's trials) as later told everywhere.

title: Hita Caurāsī
summary: Eighty-four Braj padas by Hita Harivaṃśa on the eternal love-play (nitya-vihāra) of Śyāmā (Rādhā) and Śyāma (Kṛṣṇa) in the groves of Vṛndāvana, witnessed by the sakhīs; the scripture of the Rādhāvallabha sampradāya.

title: Rādhā-sudhānidhi (Rādhā-rasa-sudhānidhi)
summary: About 270 Sanskrit verses of praise and longing addressed to Rādhā as the supreme goddess of love, whose favour even Kṛṣṇa seeks; recited in both the Rādhāvallabha and Gauḍīya traditions.

attribution.tradition: The Rādhāvallabhīs ascribe it to Hita Harivaṃśa; the Gauḍīyas to Prabodhānanda Sarasvatī.

title: Sphuṭ Vāṇī (of Hita Harivaṃśa)
summary: Miscellaneous padas and verses of Hita Harivaṃśa outside the Hita Caurāsī.

title: Sevak Vāṇī
summary: Verses of Sevak (Dāmodardās), an early disciple-poet of the Rādhāvallabha tradition, praising Hita Harivaṃśa and the principle of hita (love).

title: Bayālīs Līlā (of Dhruvadās)
summary: Forty-two short works by Dhruvadās expounding Rādhāvallabha rasa-theology: the eternal love of the pair, the sakhīs' service, and hita as the essence of all.

title: Vyās Vāṇī
summary: Padas and sākhīs of Harirām Vyās of Orchhā, a Vṛndāvana poet associated with the Rādhāvallabha circle, on the pair's love and the true devotee.

attribution.scholarly: 16th c.; his sectarian affiliation is claimed by more than one sampradāya.

title: Kelimāl
summary: One hundred and ten songs by Svāmī Haridās on the natural, eternal pair (sahaja jorī) Kuñjabihārī and Śyāmā at play in the grove (nikuñja), sung in dhrupad style; the scripture of the Haridāsī tradition.

title: Aṣṭādaśa Siddhānta (Siddhānta ke pada) of Svāmī Haridās
summary: Eighteen doctrinal songs by Svāmī Haridās: live as Hari keeps you, do not delay the name while death hunts with drawn bow, the world's pursuits are empty.

title: Mīrā Padāvalī
summary: The songs ascribed to Mīrābāī: love for Giridhar Gopāl as her only husband, defiance of family honour (lok-lāj), the pain of separation, the poison sent by the Rāṇā, the saints' company, and the name as treasure. Sung across north and west India.

attribution.scholarly: Only a handful of songs appear in manuscripts before the 18th c.; most of the corpus is attributed, composed and reshaped by singers in her name.

tradition.text: Mīrā's lifetime (tradition: c. 1498–1547)

scholarly.text: 16th c. core (small) with extensive later accretion

title: Kīrtana-ghoṣā
summary: The central scripture of the Ekaśaraṇa tradition: Śaṅkaradeva's narrative songs for congregational singing, retelling the Bhāgavata — the avatāras, Kṛṣṇa's childhood and deeds, the rāsa, the story of Ajāmila and the power of the name, the offences against the name, the refutation of other paths — and praising the name of Kṛṣṇa as the one refuge.

attribution.tradition: Śaṅkaradeva's; gathered into one book after his death, with a few sections by other poets of his circle.
attribution.scholarly: Core by Śaṅkaradeva; compilation history and the authorship of some sections debated.

title: Nām-ghoṣā (Hājārī-ghoṣā)
summary: Mādhavadeva's thousand verses on the name and on devotion: bowing first to the devotees who do not desire even liberation, it teaches the name of Kṛṣṇa, service to the guru and the company of devotees as the whole path.

title: Bhakti-ratnākara (of Śaṅkaradeva)
summary: Śaṅkaradeva's Sanskrit anthology, mainly of Bhāgavata verses, arranged topically to set out the doctrine of exclusive devotion to Kṛṣṇa; later rendered into Assamese.
notes: Not the Bengali Gauḍīya Bhaktiratnākara of Narahari Cakravartī, nor Mādhavadeva's Bhakti-ratnāvalī.

title: Bhakti-ratnāvalī (of Viṣṇupurī)
summary: Viṣṇupurī's Sanskrit anthology of Bhāgavata verses on devotion, arranged by the forms of devotion; the basis of Mādhavadeva's Assamese rendering.

title: Bhakti-ratnāvalī (Assamese, of Mādhavadeva)
summary: Mādhavadeva's Assamese verse rendering of Viṣṇupurī's Bhakti-ratnāvalī, expounding the forms of devotion with hearing and singing foremost.

title: Bargīt (Borgeet)
summary: The 'noble songs' of Śaṅkaradeva (some thirty-four survive) and Mādhavadeva (well over a hundred) in Brajabuli, set to classical rāgas and sung at the opening of sattra services: dispassion, the name, and the child Kṛṣṇa.

attribution.tradition: Śaṅkaradeva composed many more (traditionally 240), most lost in a fire.

title: Cihna-yātrā
summary: Śaṅkaradeva's first dramatic performance, staged with painted scenes of the seven Vaikuṇṭhas; the text is lost. Performed as bhāonā with a sūtradhāra who sings, dances and explains.

title: Patnī-prasāda
summary: Aṅkīyā nāṭ on the Brahmin wives who fed Kṛṣṇa against their husbands' ritual scruples: devotion over ritual. Performed as bhāonā with a sūtradhāra who sings, dances and explains.

title: Kāliya-damana
summary: Aṅkīyā nāṭ on Kṛṣṇa's subduing of the serpent Kāliya. Performed as bhāonā with a sūtradhāra who sings, dances and explains.

title: Keli-gopāla
summary: Aṅkīyā nāṭ on the rāsa play of Kṛṣṇa with the gopīs. Performed as bhāonā with a sūtradhāra who sings, dances and explains.

title: Rukmiṇī-haraṇa
summary: Aṅkīyā nāṭ on Kṛṣṇa's carrying off of Rukmiṇī. Performed as bhāonā with a sūtradhāra who sings, dances and explains.

title: Pārijāta-haraṇa
summary: Aṅkīyā nāṭ on Kṛṣṇa's bringing the pārijāta tree from heaven. Performed as bhāonā with a sūtradhāra who sings, dances and explains.

title: Rāma-vijaya
summary: Aṅkīyā nāṭ on Rāma's winning of Sītā, composed late in Śaṅkaradeva's life at the Koch court. Performed as bhāonā with a sūtradhāra who sings, dances and explains.

title: Guṇamālā
summary: The whole Bhāgavata in brief verses, said to have been composed in a single night at King Naranārāyaṇa's request.

title: Nimi-navasiddha-saṃvāda
summary: Assamese rendering of the nine sages' teaching to King Nimi (Bhāgavata 11.2–5) on the religion of the devotee (bhāgavata-dharma).

title: Bhakti-pradīpa
summary: Short work proclaiming exclusive devotion to Kṛṣṇa as superior to all other means and to the worship of other gods.

title: Anādi-pātana
summary: Assamese account of creation and the cosmic cycle, drawn from the Bhāgavata and Vāmana Purāṇa.

title: Daśama (Śaṅkaradeva's Assamese Bhāgavata X)
summary: Śaṅkaradeva's Assamese verse rendering of the tenth book of the Bhāgavata (Kṛṣṇa's life), read in the nāmghars.

title: Kathā-gurucarit
summary: A prose hagiography of Śaṅkaradeva, Mādhavadeva and their successors, narrating Śaṅkaradeva's pilgrimages, the conversion of Mādhavadeva, the brahmins' complaints before the kings and the spread of the sattras.

attribution.tradition: Compiled from the oral accounts of the devotees.

title: Guru-carita (of Rāmacaraṇa Ṭhākura)
summary: Verse life of Śaṅkaradeva by Rāmacaraṇa Ṭhākura, Mādhavadeva's nephew.

title: Śaṅkaradeva–Mādhavadeva Carita (of Daityāri Ṭhākura)
summary: Verse hagiography of the two founders by Daityāri Ṭhākura.

title: Kathā-Bhāgavata (of Bhaṭṭadeva)
summary: Bhaṭṭadeva's Assamese prose rendering of the Bhāgavata, counted the first great work of Assamese prose.

title: Kathā-Gītā (of Bhaṭṭadeva)
summary: Bhaṭṭadeva's Assamese prose rendering of the Bhagavad Gītā.

title: Narsinh Mehta's padas
summary: The songs of Narsinh Mehta of Junāgaḍh: dawn songs (prabhātiyāṃ), songs of the rāsa and of Kṛṣṇa's love, songs of non-dual knowledge ('in the whole universe you alone, Śrī Hari'), the marks of the true Vaiṣṇava, and autobiographical poems (the Hāramālā, Māmeruṃ, Huṇḍī episodes).

attribution.scholarly: Manuscripts are late (17th c. onward) and many songs are later; the core is accepted.

tradition.text: 15th c.

title: Annamācārya's saṅkīrtanas
summary: Songs of Tāḷḷapāka Annamācārya to Veṅkaṭeśvara of Tirumala — devotional (ādhyātma) and love (śṛṅgāra) songs — inscribed on copper plates by his family; they include the teaching that Brahman is one for king and servant alike.

attribution.tradition: He composed 32,000 songs; about 14,000 survive on copper plates at Tirumala.

title: Tyāgarāja's kṛtis
summary: Some seven hundred surviving songs of Tyāgarāja of Tiruvaiyāru to Rāma: surrender, the name of Rāma, the saints, and music (nāda) as a path to God when joined to devotion; they include the five 'jewel' songs (pañcaratna).

attribution.tradition: Tyāgarāja's; transmitted through his disciples' lines.

title: Prahlāda Bhakti Vijayam
summary: Tyāgarāja's musical drama on Prahlāda's devotion.

title: Naukā Caritram
summary: Tyāgarāja's musical drama on Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs' boat ride, humbling their pride.

title: Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtana
summary: Baḍu Caṇḍīdās's Middle Bengali song-narrative of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in thirteen sections (khaṇḍas), earthy and dramatic, ending in Rādhā's lament of separation.

attribution.scholarly: A single manuscript found in 1909 and published in 1916; its date and relation to the lyric 'Caṇḍīdās' are debated.

title: Caṇḍīdās padāvalī
summary: Lyrics on Rādhā's love and separation signed 'Caṇḍīdās' (the name of more than one poet), sung by Caitanya and later claimed by the Sahajiyās.

attribution.tradition: One Caṇḍīdās of Nānnur, lover of Rāmī the washerwoman.
attribution.scholarly: Several poets (Baḍu, Dvija, Dīna Caṇḍīdās); attributions unresolved.

title: Vidyāpati padāvalī
summary: Vidyāpati's Maithili songs on Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa — first love, union and separation (especially the rains) — together with his songs to Śiva (nacārī) and Gaurī; Caitanya relished them and they shaped Bengali and Assamese Brajabuli song.

attribution.scholarly: Accepted core; many songs survive only in Bengali and Nepali recensions.

title: Dāśarathi Śatakam
summary: A century of Telugu verses to Rāma, son of Daśaratha, by Kañcarla Gopanna (Bhadrācala Rāmadās).

title: Kīrtanas of Bhadrācala Rāmadās
summary: Telugu devotional songs to Rāma of Bhadrācalam, including the prison songs reproaching Rāma for his devotee's suffering.

attribution.tradition: Rāmadās's, sung in prison at Golconda.
